questions.q: Why doesn't a smart contract's on-chain trust guarantee extend to its frontend?
options: The frontend is ordinary client-side code served from ordinary infrastructure, and inherits normal web risks like a compromised build pipeline or hijacked DNS
It does extend -- a verified contract automatically verifies its frontend too
Frontends are stored on-chain and verified the same way contracts are
Wallets re-compile and verify the frontend's source code before every page load
questions.explain: A contract's guarantees come from the chain itself; the website calling it is normal web infrastructure with normal web risks.

questions.q: What does a single deploy on a platform like Vercel or Netlify typically produce for a modern dApp frontend?
options: A mix of static assets, serverless functions, and sometimes edge middleware, all versioned and rollback-able together
Only a single static HTML file
A new smart contract deployment on-chain
Nothing -- dApp frontends cannot use serverless functions
questions.explain: Most dApp frontends mix static assets with serverless functions and middleware; the platform versions all of it as one atomic, rollback-able unit.

questions.q: What is the main benefit of an automatic preview deployment for every pull request?
options: A reviewer can connect a test wallet and click through the actual proposed UI before it ever reaches production
It replaces the need for a production deployment entirely
It automatically audits the smart contract the frontend calls
It only shows a static screenshot of the proposed change, not a running app
questions.explain: A live preview URL lets a reviewer interact with the real running UI -- important when a frontend bug could mean a user signs the wrong transaction.

questions.q: Why does verifying a custom domain's DNS configuration matter even after a build succeeds?
options: Because users load the project's real domain, not a platform-generated .vercel.app or .netlify.app URL, and that's the domain they'll trust enough to connect a wallet to
Because DNS verification is required before the build can even start
Because it changes the contract address the frontend points to
It doesn't matter -- platform-generated URLs are what real users bookmark
questions.explain: A verified custom domain is the last trust boundary between a working build and something users actually load and interact with.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what comes next after hosting a dApp's frontend?
options: Containerizing indexers and backend services -- the parts of the stack that hold state and run continuously
Writing the smart contract's test suite from scratch
Returning to Chapter 1 to re-cover fuzz testing
Nothing further -- the off-chain stack is complete once the frontend is hosted
questions.explain: Lesson 19 moves to the harder half of the off-chain stack: indexers and backend services that hold state and run continuously, unlike a mostly-static frontend.
